newsitem.title: USA: Swiss guard praised at U.S. Senate hearing.
newsitem.headline: Swiss guard praised at U.S. Senate hearing.

text.p: The guard who disclosed that a Swiss bank was shredding Holocaust era documents said on Tuesday he was trying to protect Switzerland and the truth.

"I was convinced that documents were being destroyed illegally. I wished to prevent the Swiss people from suffering harm, and to make the documents and actions known to the public," Christoph Meili said at a U.S. Senate Banking Committee hearing.

In January, Meili took some documents from the shredding room of the Union Bank of Switzerland in Zurich and turned them over to a Jewish organisation which gave them to the police. He also reported that other documents dating from the Second World War were being destroyed.

Meili, 29, was suspended by the security firm Wache AG and fired last week. He said he felt he was being treated like a criminal in Switzerland and had received death threats and threats that his two children would be kidnapped.
"I also wanted the oppressed Jewish population -- the Holocaust victims -- to not again be left behind in their search for documentation at the Swiss banks and to get justice," Meili said.

"I went public about this matter because I want to testify to everyone regarding this matter in the interests of Switzerland. I have not been directed by anyone; I acted on my own decision and I have no intention of profiting from this action," he said."
Asked if he would the same thing again, Meili replied, "Yes, I would for the truth."

UBS says the destruction of records from a subsidiary it acquired in 1945 was a "regrettable accident" and insists no records were lost that could aid the search for missing assets that Hitler's victims may have deposited in Swiss banks.
Committee members called Meili a hero and condemned his treatment in Switzerland.
"You ought to be a hero in your country," Sen. Christopher Dodd, a Connecticut Democrat, told Meili.

"While Christoph and his family have been persecuted for his noble deed, it is a disgrace that the bank's archivist who ordered the shredding at UBS, Erwin Haggenmuller, still has his job and faces no prosecution," Chairman Alfonse D'Amato, a New York Republican, said.
Israel Singer of the World Jewish Congress said Meili had been offered a job on Monday by the organisation.

Separately, the State Department said it would release a report on Wednesday on Nazi gold looted from Holocaust victims. Sources close to the department told Reuters last week the report would be very harsh on the Swiss role in the war as bankers and money-launderers for the Third Reich.
